procedural_history.originating_court: Special Judge, National Investigation Agency (NIA) (3rd Additional Sessions Judge) Jammu
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment rendered by the Special Judge, National Investigation Agency (NIA) (3rd Additional Sessions Judge) Jammu
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Division Bench of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir at Jammu in Criminal Appeal (D) No.11/2020 dated 27.04.2021 confirmed the judgment of the Special Judge in part, but remitted the issue pertaining to charges framed under Sections 306 and 411 of the Jammu and Kashmir State Ranbir Penal Code SVT., 1989 along with Section 39 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 for taking cognizance afresh.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant challenged the judgment of the High Court in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal.

directions: The fines if paid by the petitioners should be refunded.

It will be open to the prosecution to proceed afresh against the petitioners in respect of the charges under Ss. 384 and 384/114, I.P.C. or even as regards the charge under S. 120-B, I.P.C. provided that the requisite sanction under S. 196-A, Criminal P. C. has been duly obtained.
Such retrial, if it is to take place, will be held before some Magistrate other than the learned Magistrate who has already dealt with this case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial was vitiated because the prosecution for criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B, I.P.C. was initiated without the mandatory sanction required under Section 196-A of the Criminal Procedure Code.

facts: The petitioners were prosecuted and convicted for criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B, I.P.C., and for extortion under Sections 384 and 384/114, I.P.C.
The object of the criminal conspiracy was to commit extortion, which is a non-cognizable offense.
The prosecution for the conspiracy charge under Section 120-B was initiated without the sanction from the Local Government or District Magistrate, as required by the law.
law: Section 196-A of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) states that a court cannot take cognizance of the offense of criminal conspiracy (punishable under Section 120-B, I.P.C.) when the object of the conspiracy is to commit a non-cognizable offense, unless the prosecution is sanctioned by the appropriate government authority.
application: The Court found that since the object of the conspiracy was to commit extortion (a non-cognizable offense), the sanction required by Section 196-A, CrPC was mandatory.
As no such sanction was obtained, the court could not legally take cognizance of the conspiracy offense.
The Court rejected the prosecution's suggestion to uphold the convictions for the substantive extortion offenses alone. It reasoned that the petitioners were tried for all charges simultaneously.
A significant amount of evidence presented to prove the (improperly charged) conspiracy was likely irrelevant to the substantive extortion charges and would have prejudiced the petitioners' case.
The Court held that a trial that improperly combines charges requiring sanction with those that do not cannot be separated after the fact to salvage a conviction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the entire trial was vitiated (invalidated) due to the failure to obtain the mandatory sanction under Section 196-A of the CrPC. Consequently, the Court set aside the convictions and sentences for all charges. It allowed the prosecution the option to proceed with a fresh trial, provided they first obtained the requisite sanction for the conspiracy charge.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial was vitiated because the prosecution for criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B, I.P.C. was initiated without the mandatory sanction required under Section 196-A of the Criminal Procedure Code.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 had come into force, which made the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 applicable, and therefore the judgment of the High Court (which likely quashed the proceedings for lack of sanction under the old code) should be set aside.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the law prevailing at the time the complaint was made, the Jammu & Kashmir Criminal Procedure Code, 1989 (CrPC, 1989), was applicable.
Under the CrPC, 1989, the requisite sanction under Section 196-A was mandatory for prosecuting a charge of criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B, I.P.C.
The respondent contended that the new procedural law (CrPC, 1973) could not be applied retrospectively to cure the defect of lack of sanction.

statutes.act_name: Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation (Removal of Difficulties) Order, 2019

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court cannot take cognizance of the offense of criminal conspiracy to commit a non-cognizable offense without the requisite sanction from the appropriate government authority as mandated by Section 196-A of the Criminal Procedure Code. A trial conducted without such sanction is vitiated.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Because the object of the criminal conspiracy was to commit a non-cognizable offence (extortion under S. 384, I.P.C.), the court could not legally take cognizance of the conspiracy charge under S. 120-B, I.P.C. without the mandatory prior sanction from the Local Government as required by Section 196-A of the Criminal Procedure Code. This failure to obtain sanction vitiated the trial.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a court can take cognizance of an offence of criminal conspiracy (S. 120-B, I.P.C.) to commit a non-cognizable offence without the prior sanction of the Local Government or a designated District Magistrate, as mandated by Section 196-A of the Criminal Procedure Code.
why_appellant_lost: The prosecution failed to obtain the mandatory sanction under Section 196-A, Criminal P.C. before initiating proceedings for criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B, I.P.C., which was a fatal procedural flaw.

The prosecution's suggestion to salvage the convictions on the substantive charges (S. 384 and 384/114, I.P.C.) was rejected because the trial on those charges was inextricably linked with the improperly brought conspiracy charge, creating prejudice against the accused.
why_respondent_won: The court could not legally take cognizance of the criminal conspiracy charge without the requisite sanction under S. 196-A, Criminal P.C., rendering the trial on that charge invalid from the outset.

The court determined that the trial held on charges that do not require sanction (extortion) alongside a charge that was not cognizable without sanction (conspiracy) could not be separated, as evidence for the invalid conspiracy charge likely prejudiced the trial on the other charges.
policy_considerations: It is prejudicial to an accused person to uphold convictions on some charges when the trial for those charges was conducted jointly with a more serious charge that was improperly before the court. Evidence adduced to establish the charge of conspiracy, which would not have been relevant for the substantive charges alone, may have unfairly influenced the outcome.

A trial held on charges which do not require sanction along with charges that are not cognizable without sanction under S. 196-A, Criminal P. C., cannot be separated after the fact to cure the defect, as this would result in prejudice to the petitioners.
